utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Seems to have been a little confusion this morning at the change of courtrooms, which I did mention last night before we broke. This morning Judge Baird is not feeling well. It is hoped that he will be able to join us during the morning but whether that can happen or not, we will continue to sit under Rule 15 bis. If we could have the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I remind you that the affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies, and Mr. Djurdjic is continuing his questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Examination in chief by Mr. Djurdjic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we may, I would like to continue where we left off yesterday and that is the organisational chart drawn by the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can I tender this hard copy now of the diagram into evidence, or should we use the machine?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will be getting some explanation of this diagram, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, could you please explain the diagram that you have drawn for us.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to apologise because it doesn't look so great, but it was not the best way to draw it on the desk with the binder underneath, but in any case, this command diagram is considerably different from the one that I saw yesterday drawn by somebody from the Prosecutor's Office. What exactly is the difference? The main thing is that the Supreme Defence Council in peacetime is the Supreme Command in war time headed by the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia who pursuant to the constitution and the law and we heard the appropriate articles commands in peacetime and war time the Army of Yugoslavia in accordance to the Supreme Defence Council. In that sense, at the strategic level, you have the Supreme Command staff as the professional staff organ of the Supreme Command, that's why it's called the Supreme Command staff. It this is headed by the Chief of the Supreme Command staff, so that is one level of commanding. As we can see, the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that box has two lines leading down because the president commands the strategic groups as the supreme commander, so the president of the FRY, the supreme commander, commands the 1st, 2nd, and the 3rd Army, the navy, and the air force and anti-aircraft Defence. Then you have a dotted line underneath the Chief of the Supreme Command staff because he can pursuant to decision by the Supreme Command also issues orders, tasks to the strategic groups pursuant to the decisions of the supreme commander and the Supreme Command. The difference between this diagram and the one we saw yesterday lies in the fact that there we have a separate level of command, the Supreme Defence Council, the Supreme Command are separate and then underneath that you have the Supreme Command staff and Chief of Staff. That would mean that these are two separate levels of command and would imply that the Supreme Command would have to have considerably more people in order to be able to put into practice the decisions of the supreme commander pursuant to conclusions of the Supreme Defence Council. So there is a considerable difference there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to ask you this: We see the strategic groups here. Within the 3rd Army would you be able to tell us what were the subordinate organisational units there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both in peace time and war time, there were a number of them. At this point I'm just going to focus on the war time situation and if necessary, I can also provide explanations for circumstances in peacetime. The 3rd Army commander had under his command the following units: The Nis Corps, the Pristina Corps, the Nis Military District and the Pristina military district; some independence and staff units such as the armour unit, communications regiment, reconnaissance units, military police units and so on, and we also had two logistics bases: One was in Nis for the territory covered by the Nis Corps that provided materiel and equipment to all the Nis Corps units and other units in that area, and one base in Kosovo and Metohija or in Pristina which served the logistics needs of all the units that were located in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me how the chain of command functioned in the Army of Yugoslavia in the course of 1999?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During 1999, we have two periods which would be of interest for this Court. The first one was from the 1st of January until the 24th of March, and the second one from the 24th of March until the 20th of June. The chain of command was the one defined by the laws and the constitution so the Supreme Command council in peace time; in war time the supreme commander commanded the strategic groups directly or through the Chief of the Supreme Command staff or the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in the Supreme Defence Council. Yesterday we looked at the composition so we know that. Who had the right of decision-making in the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I spoke in more detail about the Supreme Defence Council, but I am going to just say one sentence. The Supreme Defence Council, according to the constitution, comprised the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the president of the Republic of Serbia, and the president of the Republic of Montenegro. That was the full composition and the only composition of the Supreme Defence Council. Let me add also, all of these members, these three presidents, made the decisions and agreed on matters, and whatever they agreed on then the president of the FRY then formulated that into orders, commands and so on and so forth. In war time, that was the Supreme Command. That body. Since I did say we had two periods which is up until the 24th of March and after the 24th of March, so exclusively through the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Chief of the Supreme Command staff orders went down to commanders of the strategic formations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware if any other persons attended meetings of the Supreme Defence Council and if yes, what was their role?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware that from time to time depending on the topic that was being discussed at the Supreme Defence Council, the president of the Supreme Defence Council would invite certain people to attend. Most frequently it was the minister of defence that was invited, the prime minister, the Chief of the General Staff and some other ministers depending on the sphere or the topic that was being discussed. These persons could not participate in the decision-making or the voting. These persons were only there to reply to questions and to propose. I know this amongst other things because I occasionally participated in the preparation of the material for the Chief of General Staff. That would be used for the meeting of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in two things, but we can take it one by one. First of all, during the aggression, how did the communication proceed between the Supreme Command staff and the Chief of Staff with the Supreme Defence Council? Are you informed about that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that the Supreme Command and the Supreme Command staff is one body. They were at the same location, the same command post. So where we were in the Supreme Command staff that is also where the Supreme Command was. I know that they were in contact on a daily basis and that the Chief of the Supreme Command staff had the unit at least once a day to meet and to see members of the Supreme Defence Council who were at the command post. They communicated probably by telephone, even though it was only that they were two floors apart, or they also communicated through the military cabinets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please inform us a little bit more about the reporting to the members of the Supreme Defence Council during the aggression and even before 1999, how were they informed?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the aggression every morning by 6.00 a.m. the combat report that we had the opportunity to see yesterday was provided to the military cabinet of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and it was for the president of Yugoslavia and also for the president of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic. There was a separate report, I mean the same report was sent to other persons that usually received such reports primarily it was sent to the minister of defence who was not at the command post. The president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would read the report by 8.00 and the attachments, and at that time around 8.00 a.m. he would call or would go himself to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command to discuss the situation. I know this because this is something that the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command General Ojdanic told me several times that he would be surprised that the president had studied the report and the attachments especially reports of the 3rd Army command that were sent as attachments. He would put some questions only that needed to be clarified because he was more or less familiar with the situation on the basis of the written report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you are now retired. Let me ask you this: When a military person and a general is retired, does he have access to documents of military nature that are now topical that are part of the current work?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Although I'm a lieutenant-general and used to work in that first administration, I do not have access to any document short of passing through a special procedure. Nobody has the right to share documents with third parties even if these third parties are retired generals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, are there any rules in the Army of Yugoslavia, were there any rules when you were active, about the safekeeping and archiving of documents?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are rules of office management concerning the drafting of documents and safekeeping and archiving of documents. Every document that is produced is recorded in the register and so is every document received from another command. At the end of the year, all of these are archived, only originals though. And another thing, the Chief of the Supreme Command staff ordered on the 23rd of April, 1999 when a state of immediate threat of war was proclaimed that a special register should be opened to register all the incoming and ongoing documents, and that stayed in place until the 20th of June, 1999. At the same time, the Chief of the Supreme Command staff ordered that all these documents, all these originals be kept and collected into archives at the end of the war. Under that written order from the Chief of the Supreme Command staff, I was tasked with organising the archiving of all documents from the Supreme Command staff and all the documents that the Supreme Command staff received from subordinate units. Let me emphasise that at the command post 1 register was kept at the office administration, and that is where all the documents were logged. Ingoing and -- incoming and outgoing. There was another register in the office of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff because various parties such as ministers, politicians, businessmen often met with him and addressed him, and that's why this register was kept. Another service, namely the security administration, had its own register.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, would the fact that a stamp of the archives is found on a certain document mean that the document is authentic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. Depends on some other elements, although I would like to explain this using a specific example. If there are no other stamps or signatures, and I would be able to establish that as a professional, then the document would still not be authentic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you asked for an example I would like to take you back to two documents we saw today. One of them is dated 25 of May 1999 sent by the 3rd Army to the Supreme Command staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's P888.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your binder it's 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before we move on, are you going to deal with this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We dealt only with -- oh, you mean the diagram? Thank you, Your Honours. I tender the diagram drawn by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could the display again show the diagram, please. Thank you. Before we receive it, I need to get a couple of things more clear. VSO-VK, what does that stand for? What is that the abbreviation for? Could you help us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] VSO is Supreme Defence Council. It's the Supreme Command in war time. Supreme Defence Council equals Supreme Command in war time. And then we see an acronym for the Supreme Command staff and VK means Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Below that you have, I believe, the president of the federal republic on your diagram. He was the president of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was also chairman or president of the Supreme Defence Council and from that we drew the conclusion that he was also the supreme commander in war time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The other members of the Defence Council that you mentioned are the presidents of Serbia and Montenegro; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In peacetime, did that Supreme Defence Council exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and it was convened from time to time at the request of the president, and it also had a standing secretary General Susic who kept minutes, records, produced documents, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In peacetime, could the Supreme Defence Council issue orders to the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that both in peacetime and in war time, the armies under the command of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in keeping with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, therefore the Supreme Defence Council as a collective body did not issue assignments and tasks. That was done by the president in peacetime and in war time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would understand that at some time earlier than March of 1999, the Supreme Defence Council comprised the presidents of the different republics of Serbia as well as the president of the federal republic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I did not quite understand because at that time there were only two republics, Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There must have been at some time presidents of Croatia, for example, Slovenia. Were they parts of the Supreme Defence Council? Were they members of it at a time earlier than March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps ten years before that. Until 1991 there was a body called the Supreme Command. And presidents of all republics, Slovenia, Macedonia, Croatia, et cetera were represented on it. The president of Yugoslavia was at the head. However, after the break-up, after 1991, they did not participate any longer in the work of this body, the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I ask the questions in that way because it seems to me that the Supreme Defence Council was a body that brought together the political heads of the different components of the federal republic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And as you say in 1999, there were the republics of Serbia and of Montenegro as well as the president of the federal republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, also on your diagram below the president of the federal republic you have SVK. Could you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This acronym which is actually SVK is there because the General Staff was actually the staff body for preparing, organising, and executing combat activity. The acronym means Supreme Command staff. It was the staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the president of the -- or the chairman of the Supreme Defence Council, that is the president of the federal republic, by decision of the Supreme Defence Council wished to issue an order to all or some of the strategic elements of the army, would the staff that you have designated there prepare that order for the president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that staff was headed by the Chief of the Supreme Command staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At the head of this Supreme Command staff was a chief, specifically Colonel Dragomir Ojdanic, who before that was Chief of the General Staff. And in war time, he became Chief of the Supreme Command staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've already answered my next question. The Chief of the General Staff and the Chief of the Supreme Command staff were in fact the same person, they just changed names when war was declared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, below the SVK you have another box. What is that? Nacelnik SVK it appears to be or some such, you'll have to pardon my Serbian pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following the same procedure, the same logic, when I said that the person number one in the Supreme Command was the president of Yugoslavia, I also tried to explain that the Chief of the General Staff was at the head of the Supreme Command staff under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So that lower box is the Chief of the Supreme Command staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In peacetime, is it really the effect of what you are saying that the Supreme Command -- sorry, the Supreme Defence Council rarely met, so for the most part it was for the General Staff to command the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Supreme Defence Council met in peacetime, and as far as I know, there are stenographic minutes from all the meetings of the Supreme Defence Council. I had occasion to see them. In peacetime, the General Staff did its job based on those decisions and the decisions of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia who was supreme commander. Now, considering that the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command executed many tasks in the army on behalf of the president, he headed this body and that's why he is represented on the diagram with an interrupted line because the exclusive right to command the army in peacetime and in war time belonged to the president of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It seems to me that the effect of what you are saying really is that there were changes of name in war time, and maybe the Supreme Defence Council became much more active, but really there was no fundamental change to the command structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, or rather, no, there was no change in the structure, but there was a change of name, and the Supreme Command staff was much smaller than the General Staff was in peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's a very interesting observation on efficiency. I noted that in your evidence earlier. The president of the federal republic held his authority as president of the Supreme Defence Council; is that correct? His authority to command the army was because he was president of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and because the Law on Defence in certain articles that we read yesterday, I believe, it is stipulated that he is the only one who is entitled to command the army in peacetime and in war time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you can help me as well. Were the prime minister of the federal republic and the republics of Serbia and Montenegro and the minister of defence of the federal republic not involved in this structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid you misunderstood me. Only the minister of defence does not belong in this body. This body includes the president of Yugoslavia, the president of Serbia, the president of Montenegro. They are the three members of the Supreme Defence Council. The minister of the Defence, the Chief of the General Staff, and the federal minister are invited occasionally to discuss specific matters at the Supreme Defence Council, and they do not have the right of vote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question of Judge Fluegge arises from a comment you made earlier. You would understand the prime minister and the president to be the same person, or a separate person? Two different people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The president is one thing, and the federal prime minister is another thing. Sometimes, and that may cause confusion, we call prime minister president of the government. He was invited occasionally to the sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, but they were not -- the presidents of the governments of the Federal Republic Serbia and Montenegro were not by the law members of the Supreme Defence Council? They could be invited to attend; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know of a single case when prime ministers, that is presidents of the governments of the constituent republics, were invited to a session of the Supreme Defence Council. We have somewhat a different attitude towards prime ministers. The president of a republic represents the republic, and the prime minister probably plays a more modest role than in western countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. What about the minister for defence? Was he not part of this structure, the chain of command? Didn't he take part in any decisions or meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. He is not in this chain of command. He is subordinated to the federal prime minister. He has civilian authority and the civilian supervisor of the army. He may attend certain sessions depending on the subject matter, in which case he would be invited and provided with background material in good time, and he may participate in discussion, but he does not have the right of vote. That's how it was according to the constitution and the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This diagram drawn by the witness will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit Number D00566. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, I interrupted you, you were moving on, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After questions like this, it's almost a shame for me to continue. I had asked for a document though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 32, General.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I found it, but maybe you could sort of clear the screen so I could follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness see the document on the -- sorry, could the witness look at the transcript instead of the document. You don't have to look at me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is a report from the 3rd command -- 3rd Army command, 25 May 1999, strictly confidential, 872-94/1-2. There's no stamp that it was archived. If this document found its way into the archives, could we establish when it was created?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my humble opinion, this document could never find its way into the archives because it's not complete. It's true that there is a number and the time on the first page which tells us something about its provenance, but on the second page, certain elements that would make the document acceptable and valid are missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask for the second page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may go on.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I also see the -- yeah, thank you. It's the same as my hard copy. There is a signature, there is a stamp, but I cannot say whether it's real or not, but there is evidence in the form of stamp and date that this document arrived at the command of the -- at the Supreme Command staff, and it was registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1505 is the next document I would like to request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, sir, we can see the document. It's a telegram of the 4th of June, 1999, from the 3rd Army command sent to the Supreme Command staff, ground forces sector. Could you please look at the document and then tell us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that's happening, Mr. Djurdjic, we don't know the number of the previous document. Is it an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P88, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, it's P888. That's the previous document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, looking at this telegram again, what can you tell us as to its authenticity?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. The document has something that the other one does not have that does not have enough elements to for me to be able to assert that it is a valid one; namely, there is no signature of the commander, there is no signature by the Chief of Staff, there is no stamp that would certify each of the signatures, that of the commander and that of the Chief of Staff. There is no rectangular stamp at the bottom indicating the time of dispatch, the time of receipt, and the time it was received at the Supreme Command staff. So that stamp that is there, I can tell that it's the archives stamp, that's possible, but a document like this should not have and must not have been accepted into the archive. I note that it was my administration that was responsible for the collection of all the documents, our documents from the Supreme Command staff and subordinate archives before they were handed over to the archives, so all the war time documentation was handed into the archive so my chief would not accept or pass on to the archives a document of this type. There is something else that I've noticed. The heading of this document says, 3rd Army command, ground forces sector. You can see that ground forces sector, reading it quickly in this telegram, that would not be the sector authorised to deal with these questions. Underneath that when it says, Reference, SVK and then strictly confidential 03/ and so on and so forth, I know because the recording of documents was in my jurisdiction, so the ground forces sector is -- has the marking 02. 03 is the air force and anti-aircraft defence sector, so it's not clear why they would be sending it to the ground forces sector, but the reference would be to the air force, and the operations staff and the operations administration would be writing to subordinate organs. When you analyse this you can very quickly see that this is a telegram which even has some seven or eight addressees to whom it would be dispatched. Not everyone is authorised for ammunition, for artillery, for some unrest among the population, the role of certain officials in disbanding units and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir, just one thing, regardless of this discrepancy as to whom it was sent and so on, had it be been received by the Supreme Command staff, would this be noted or marked on this document regardless of the organisational unit?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in any case there would be a stamp, a date, a number indicating that it was received and when it was received in the Supreme Command staff. A telegram like this, if it is authentic, I conclude that it was not received, and I do not remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Had such a telegram been expedited from the 3rd Army, would it have to have an indication that it was dispatched?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would have to have a stamp, the time, the date, indicating when it was dispatched, when it was processed, when it arrived at the Supreme Command staff and so on and so forth. We had the opportunity to see yesterday during previous documents my previous testimony what such a document was supposed to look like so we did have proper examples of such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at document 65 ter Defence list 871 or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you move on, Mr. Djurdjic, I wonder whether the Chamber can be assisted more. Two documents now, Exhibit P888 and P1505. The witness has said things which indicate that he can't confirm that it is authentic. Is the witness saying that what we are looking at may be a document that was not properly dealt with at the time, or is he saying this is not a real document? There's something that suggests that it is not authentic. Is the witness saying something about either of those things, or what is he saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was afraid to put a question like that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, sir, could you respond to the question put by His Honour Judge Parker.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to be very cautious regarding the previous one, I don't remember the number of the 25th of May, that telegram I assert did not reach the General Staff while I was at the General Staff because definitely I would have seen it, familiarised myself with it, and would have had to react pursuant to it. As for this telegram, all I'm saying is that I did not see, we did not discuss it, and it was not included in our analysis and that the evening collegium during war time and sometime later, neither of the telegrams were discussed. What can be drawn as a conclusion on the basis of that is something that I am leaving up to the Court, and perhaps the Prosecutor will also have the opportunity to deal with this in more detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's the difficulty, you see. These both appear to be routine documents of the Yugoslav Army, I think in each case documents that emanate from the 3rd Army. And you are either saying, well, this is a document which didn't comply in all respects with what was normal and proper, and I don't remember seeing it at the Supreme Command staff, or is it that it could be the case that this was not a document at the time at all and for some reason, by some means within the army it has been created since May and June of 1999? It's a document from within your army, and we need some guidance whether this is a document that existed at the time, although it may have been imperfectly dealt with under administrative arrangements, or alternatively, whether this is a document that appears not to be genuine? Are you able to help us about that, you may not be able to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try, but there are a lot of questions that I have. First of all, these are not usual documents by format, the typing, the signature, the items, and so on and so forth, but since some very important things are missing proving that the document was received, then I can openly say that this did not arrive at the General Staff at that time in 1999. I recall the first one definitely, and this one too was never discussed. How can you believe that it is usual that neither the commander nor the Chief of Staff did not sign the second page of this document? We don't see it here, but perhaps we could look at the second page of this document, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show us page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, excellent. This document without any signatures, without the initials of the person who typed it, without a stamp, how can this be -- the document then be considered as an authentic document? I say that it cannot be considered authentic. Beneath this stamp you would need to have another stamp about the encryption where it would indicate when the document was dispatched, when it was received, then you would also need to have a rectangular stamp with the register number from the administration, operations administration indicating the number it was recorded under. I can show you or look at a number of properly processed documents and then on the basis of that you could clearly see what is missing in this document. On the basis of that, I conclude that it is an improper document and not an authentic one. The archive stamp at the top right-hand corner that is there does not really say anything and cannot compensate for the lack of these other verification stamps. Perhaps I hope that we will look at another document that contains all the proper elements and then I can point out to them -- point them out and say yes, they exist on that document but on this one, however, they are not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying that telegrams were signed before they were sent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you could not send a telegram unless it was signed by the person who wrote it because I could send a telegram on behalf of the commander, the Chief of Staff. The encryption department has to have the signature proving that that was the signature of the person sending or ordering the telegram. We have the situation here that the 3rd Army command resorted to a signature by some other person. For example, what it says here is the telegram can be sent, and it's then -- below that it says, Chief of Staff, Major-General Ljubisa Stojmirovic. He was the second ranking person in the staff so then you had this option, but in that case General Stojmirovic would have had to sign it so that the telegram could have been dispatched. Again I say some other elements are missing here, and I'm saying that if we encounter those in other elements during my testimony I can point them out to you so then you can see exactly what indicated that a telegram was sent from the 3rd Army command and received by the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The technology that you are used to may be different from what I was familiar with. I can understand that at the 3rd Army the commander or the author or his second in command would sign a document intended to be send by telegram to the Supreme Command, but the signed document, in my understanding, would remain at the 3rd Army and what would be sent would be a telegram that did not include the original signatures. Do I have a wrong idea about the technology?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you didn't misunderstand the technology, but I would like to clarify. If we take that variant, then in that case the original signed telegram had to be in the encryption department until the encryptions officer completed his work and dispatched the telegram. Once it arrived at the end user, the original of the telegram with the stamp and the signature would be returned to the archive. So in that case, we would have the opportunity to look at the original document from the army command which is original. Here it's not the original document, it wasn't archived, this is some sort of copy. I don't know how it came about, how it came to where it came, and I still stand by my assertion that it is not a valid copy. Perhaps I could help by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Sorry to be -- Mr. Djurdjic, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, excellent intervention. Let us clarify, General.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document will have the stamps and all of that, but His Honour Judge Parker asked you very nicely, the first copy I don't call that a telegram, I call that a text that has to be dispatched with the teleprinter or some other machine. I call it the first copy or the original. Does that have to be signed by the author when it arrives at the encryption station?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I may --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, let me continue. You can add some things later. Do we see any signature on the document that we are looking at now?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can this copy be that first original copy on the basis of which a document is dispatched from the communications centre?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, this copy that we see, had it been sent from the communication centre of the 3rd Army, what would it need to have at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at liberty to leaf through the document. Forgive me for not answering directly, but in tab 23, we have a similar example from the 3rd Army --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's tab 23 in my binder, and if you can call document on the -- on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have that, Your Honours, as D204, and can we look at that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see the document, go ahead and you can explain.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise again, but I knew that we did have documents like that. This is an original authentic valid document. We have the signature of the commander. We have the stamp of the 3rd Army next to the commander's signature. We have the addressee, and at the bottom we have the rectangular telegram where it states when it was dispatched, received, processed, and another stamp proving all of that and then at the end in the upper right-hand corner we have the stamp of the archive. We did not have any of those other elements except for the archive stamp in the document that we were looking at just now, and the document of the 25th of May. I'm going to be happy and satisfied if I've helped to understand the difference, and I think the difference is very evident between the first, second, and the third document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What you have just said at the end, is that something that you read from the stamp? Did you read the time of dispatch and the date? I think you said something else that was under the signature.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is indicated on the stamp. It's stamped. The time of the telegram was received at 1055 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's all I wanted to hear you made a lapse so it's been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now can we look at P1505.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now look at this option: Expediting a telegram from the 3rd Army, then it arrives at the Supreme Command staff. What would that copy of the telegram, the one that was received, have to contain?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than the things that we have seen and this is evidence that this is the first copy from the 3rd Army, once that arrives at the Supreme Command staff or some other address, it would need to have the stamp, the date of its registration in the log-book, that it was received at the address or the Supreme Command staff. We have such stamps so I'm going to perhaps point them out if we encountered such one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can we look at your tab 27 and 871 on the 65 ter list, and that is exhibit or document 405265 of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's P1449 I have just been told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, sir, have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see here that a document was sent from the 3rd Army command on the 20th of April, 1999. It's a telegram. With respect to the suggestions, can we now look at page 2 of the document in order to comment on it in respect of the previous question. Can you please read this text, I do have a question about it. General, sir, is the term "joint command" mentioned anywhere in this telegram?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just reading through the document quickly, I did not come up with the term "joint command."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Since in the previous transcript we have something like this, let's look at page 2 of this document, and can you please comment regarding the previous question about how the document was received and what was then noted later or subsequently?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm going to disappoint you a little bit with my answer. We don't have everything that we would need to have because this is a again an example from the 3rd Army and not one that was received by the General Staff; namely, we do have a stamp here when this was sent at 1155 hours when it was processed, when it was received at 1205 hours, however, this is evidence for the encryption -- of encryption in the 3rd Army. What do we have underneath that? The addressees. This is something that was added by the person received -- who received the telegram. The telegram was sent to the chief -- the deputy -- the assistant Chief of the Supreme Command staff, and it was supposed to be sent to the chief of the operations administration and the chief of the ground forces administration, and they were supposed to be informed of the contents of this telegram in order to be able to react. The stamp at the bottom without the without the date, however, is proof by Colonel Vujic that the copy reflects the original when the telegram was sent, and I see the familiar number in the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document D006-0389, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is tab 28 in your binder, General, sir. I apologise. Can you just briefly tell us whether this is again a document pertaining to the Rogovo sector, and what does this order refer to?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall discussing the matter of Rogovo at least on two occasions, sometime on the 18th of May. No, I apologise, on the 17th and the 18th of April and here on the 20th of May. We needed here to repeat our order to the commander of the 3rd and the 2nd Army to organise joint action in the area where the 2nd and 3rd Army overlapped because evidently the Rogovo action from the telegram of the 17th was not implemented correctly, and it had to be repeated again. We are pointing out to them what we wrote previously and what the chief of the staff ordered earlier to organise close co-operation in order to prevent the terrorists from spilling over into the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could I tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As document Exhibit Number D00567. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at document D006-0779, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is tab 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please turn to page 54 in Serbian and page 40 in English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an overview of the archives of the Army of Yugoslavia for the years 1998, 1999, sir. General, under number 112, I would like to ask you to tell us what type of document that is, who drafted it. We can see that the date is there.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Next to number 112, this is page 50 in my document. It states that the type of document, this is in column 2, it says that it's a suggestion. Then column 3 indicates that this was sent by the Supreme Command staff. The classification is strictly confidential. The number is 01/ --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is unable to see the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 014801, then we have a brief content, and it says, The suggestion to the commander of the 3rd Army to take measures to consolidate the 7th Infantry Brigade, so in brackets there are six specific proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly during the war there were several documents phrased as proposals.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge this is certainly not the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much. I have no further questions, Your Honours, and I tender this document. The English version is page 40. The number should be 112.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit Number D00568. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's time for the break, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, we must have the first break now. It will take 30 minutes for the tapes. We will resume at 5 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, I didn't thank you for your assistance during that evidence. Thank you. We now turn to Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I apologise to both the Trial Chamber and Ms. Petersen, I would just like the combat report that we agreed on with the Prosecution to be admitted into evidence, and it has also been made available to the Registry and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. A number will be provided later for that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Good morning, General Curcin. Without giving a -- you don't need to give a specific address, but generally, where were you physically during the NATO intervention?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, good day. At least that's what we say in our parts instead of good morning because we rise earlier probably. During the NATO intervention for the first few days I was in the building of the General Staff. However, after the first air-strikes, I personally went to the command post of the Supreme Command staff where my friends, associates, and superiors were already. So throughout the war I was at the command post of the Supreme Command staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. And just so you know, there may be a moment after you answer a question where I don't speak yet, it's just because I'm waiting for the translation to catch up, so just in case there's a pause, that's what it is. Now during the NATO intervention, did you visit Kosovo at all?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have a single opportunity in my tenure as head of the first administration to go to Kosovo, especially not during the NATO aggression because my job required me to be at the command post all the time. There were many of my colleagues which, according to plans and various assignments, had to go to Kosovo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: General, do you know the accused in this case, Vlastimir Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, do I know him? Do I know him personally?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, let's break it down, sir. Did you know him in your official capacities?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know Mr. Djordjevic personally. I think we met once at some official reception and greeted each other like all people did at the large reception sometime in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say that you knew who he was and his position, but you didn't know him personally?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew from the media who he was, and I knew his position.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could now turn to Defence 65 ter 509. If the Defence could possibly help with one of the ID numbers that could help bring this up. Line has it. Okay, it is D008-2943. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: General, this is one of those combat reports that you spoke about yesterday, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so because I see only the first page. It would be important for me to see the second page as well, if you intend to ask question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could please go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last page.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are obviously at cross purposes. Not the second, third, or fourth, but the last page of the text where the necessary elements for me to establish what it is would be. Is this the last page?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: General, I actually have a hard copy of this. Perhaps that would help if the usher could hand this to the general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my learned friend. You said that he looked at that document yesterday. Do you mean the form of the document or this precise document? Because this document, I can tell by date, was not shown yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I just meant combat reports in general. Not that this is a specific one that you saw, but that this is one of the combat reports, the type of which you spoke of yesterday. And if this could be handed to the witness, perhaps that would assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Is this the combat report, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the combat report number 28 from the Supreme Command staff dated 21st April, 1999 and now I see the attachments and the last page, and I can be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If you look at the third page of this, and it's paragraph 2.4 where it discusses the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could just go to page 3 in both B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Under section 2.4, the second paragraph, and I'll just read this out so we have it on the record. It says: "Between 19 and 20 April 1999, about 3.000 people crossed from Kosovo and Metohija to the Republic of Macedonia through the Pristina Corps 78th motorised Brigade 3rd Battalion combat disposition along the Presevo-Miratovac-Lojane axis, organised and escorted by the Presevo MUP." My question to you, sir, is basically what this is reporting is that this column of refugees had MUP officers or MUP police officers travelling alongside it, is that what we can gather from this report?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on this report, several conclusions that can be made, not just the one. First of all --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I'm just asking about the one thing, we don't need to go into more detail. I just want to know from this, can we conclude that the MUP were walking alongside or were alongside this column?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I must insist on a comprehensive answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm only interested in that one thing about this. I know there's a lot more information in this report, I'm just asking you if it appears that the MUP were alongside this column?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so and you insist an answer like this, then make your conclusion. I wanted to be of assistance. This does not apply to Kosovo. This is outside the territory of Kosovo. The 78th Brigade was defending itself in the part of Serbia outside of Kosovo. Presevo, Miratovac, and other of these places are along that axis, along the Nis Skopje road, so this does not relate to the territory of Kosovo. But you are right, and it is written there, we did not hide it, that this column passed through there and went on towards Macedonia, and it says clearly escorted by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, and it does say that these 3.000 people crossed from Kosovo to Macedonia, does it not?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we could -- I believe this probably was tendered with all of the combat reports of the Defence. If not, I would seek to tender it. It was included? Okay. Thank you. Next if we could go to P965.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you remind us of the number given to the bundle of combat reports, Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I know that, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be turned up by the Court Officer who will tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A number is yet to be assigned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can be of assistance, I believe. On this list that was submitted, it's 509. That's the Defence 65 ter number. 65 ter number 509. My learned friend also said that when she announced the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could now look at P965.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And this is the minutes of the collegium meeting held on the 11th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could look at in the English page 11, and in the B/C/S page 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: General, it appears that you are speaking here; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just ask for the text to be enlarged if I'm supposed to read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Is that you speaking, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I answer? Is that what you are asking? Yes, yes, that's my report to the Chief of the General Staff, and these are the stenographic notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to be of assistance. It's tab 10 for the general.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we look at the second paragraph after you start speaking, and I'll just read this out. It says: "The 37th Motorised Brigade" -- and in the English it says, "the ready forces of the 2nd Army, has been relocated from the Raska garrison to Kosovska Mitrovica and resubordinated to the Pristina Corps. The combat group of the 25th Nis Corps has been relocated to the Urosevac sector and resubordinated to the 243rd motorised brigade of the Pristina Corps." And if we look in English onto the next page, I believe in B/C/S it stays on page 10, two paragraphs down, you go on to say: "First in the preceding period, the commands of the strategic groups in the 2nd and 3rd Armies were given orders and permission to relocate the 37th motorised brigade of the 2nd Army and the combat group of the 21st Nis Corps and to resubordinate them to the Pristina Corps." And then skipping one paragraph and going down one more: "The order to transfer soldiers from the 1st Army, the 2nd Army, and RM navy units to the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army has been carried out under the order, 2.173 soldiers were to be transferred, and according to reports, 1,697 or 476 fewer than the number specified in the order have been transferred so far." So my question to you, sir, is: On the 11th of March, you're reporting that these transfers into the Pristina Corps have happened?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several questions there, and I'll try to take them in order. It's correct that I'm reporting about a relocation of the ready forces of the 37th motorised brigade from the Raska garrison to the Kosovska Mitrovica garrison where they were resubordinated to the Pristina Corps. The strength was 325 men, officers, and soldiers, and it's correct that this relocation took place of the combat group 21 from the Nis Corps some 75 to 80 men were moved to Urosevac. That's correct. Second, there was a question about the transfer of soldiers from the 1st and 2nd Army and the navy to the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army. I think I dealt with it in greater detail yesterday. The Chief of the General Staff had forbidden young conscripts, recruits, to be sent to Kosovo until they finished their training, and that's why the December contingent of soldiers was sent to the similar units of the 1st and 2nd Armies and the navy, to completed their training in the duration of 2 months and 23 days. Since that was completed and those soldiers were to be brought to their planned units, they were transferred by train to their units with prior notification to the OSCE Mission. First of all, the relocation of the 325 soldiers on the 37th motorised brigade and the other soldiers. Not all 2.000 and something soldiers were actually transferred, and that was because those soldiers did not arrive in Kosovo in December. Instead they were sent for training first and then on to Kosovo in March.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So, sir, it's your testimony that there was proper notification through proper channels to the OSCE Mission?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the job of other authorities. I did not deal with that personally. There was a special commission to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So you don't have firsthand knowledge of that actually happening?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not do that because it had been reported at one of the meetings because -- it had been reported at one of the meetings that it had been done, so I cannot speak from firsthand knowledge about that, I can only speak about my contributions at these meetings. But I claim that it was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Do you recall which meeting this was reported in?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we had a lot of meetings. Sometimes only a few members of the collegium met to solve a particular problem. I don't remember that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. If we could now go to 65 ter 06032. It this is a Prosecution 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, if you can just look at this, you'll see that the date on it is 6 March 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the date, but I don't see the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I do have a hard copy of this if it would be helpful for the witness. I apologise, the print is still small on the copy, but...

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And do you see that it's the 6th of March, sir, 1999?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And does this appear to be one of the things that you were reporting on at that 11th of March collegium meeting?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's our order from the first administration sent to the commands of the 1st and the 2nd Armies -- sorry, the 2nd and 3rd Armies because the 2nd Army was superior to the 37th Brigade and the 3rd Army because it was supposed to receive this units, they were notified that on day such and such the resubordination will take place. So there are all the elements there, and it speaks clearly about the peacetime complement, and it says reports on task implementation are to be delivered in one of the next documents, and from those reports you can see exactly how many men had left. And I report this because the Chief of the General Staff was aware of this as was the deputy Chief of Staff who signed in his stead. This is the usual format of an order, and I have nothing to add except if you have something specific to ask on any of the points. The document was created by us in the first administration. Colonel Gutovic created it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I will seek it to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1522. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you recall and you spoke yesterday about your testimony in the Milutinovic trial; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And during your testimony in the Milutinovic trial, you stated that you had heard mention of something called the Joint Command at a collegium meeting in January; do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And, sir, I believe in your testimony you described the Joint Command as a co-ordinating body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I answered roughly that according to what I learned later, it was a body for co-ordination between the army and the forces of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could look at your exact testimony. This is Exhibit 555 beginning at page 111, line 22. It's also, if one has the transcript, it's transcript page 17045, if that's easier. And I can just read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I believe your testimony was: "This was a body that was used for co-ordinating joint activities that were being carried out in the same area at the same time by army units and MUP units, and that's the only thing it is." Does that sound like a fair description of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot recall the exact phrasing because I answered more than one question about it, I was interrupted, and even the Trial Chamber questioned me about this so I don't know in which context I stated that. So it's obviously not in the context of the collegium meeting at the Chief of the General Staff collegium from January.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I think we need to go down to page 17045 to look at the testimony. Yeah, I guess the next page of the exhibit -- of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you reviewed this testimony before you came here today; right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't speak English, so I did have an opportunity to see the transcript generally, yes, during my preparation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, sir, yesterday, I believe that you stated you had reviewed it and the testimony was true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that I stand by everything that I stated then, and that I would give the same answers now to the same questions as I did then.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Just to make the record clear, I think we found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: It's there on page 17046 beginning at line 22 was the testimony that I referenced.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, if we could --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could now look at P1236.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you mean 17045 then, not 6?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, 17045.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And in our transcript at page 39, line 8, the last exhibit should be recorded as P1522. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could now go to P1326.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: General, do you recognise what this document is?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Are they suggestions made by General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is a document that is called "Suggestion" here sent to the 3rd Army commander personally on the 17th of April, 1999, by a set of circumstances, I participated in its drafting and then I took it for the signature of the commander at the Supreme Command staff, and after he signed, I took it to the encryption section.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And, General, in Milutinovic you testified about a map that was associated with these suggestions. Can you explain to the Court how General Ojdanic came to be in possession of the map that was associated with this?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, gladly. One evening, I can see that this was the 17th of April, I was called by the Chief of the Staff of the Supreme Command to come and see him immediately because my superior was not there at that time. The chief of the sector, General Blagoje Kovacovic. I came to his office and he showed me an excerpt from a map of ratio 1:50.000. When I say "excerpt," what I mean is that I didn't see the entire map but only a map where the top and bottom parts were cut out by scissors. I do remember that map, I remember that the Chief of the Supreme Command staff said, I just met Nesa [phoen] in the corridor a little while ago, Nesa is Lieutenant-General Nebojsa Pavkovic commander of the 3rd Army, and he was just carrying this map, he was returning from the president, I asked him what was he doing because he thought that at that time he was in Kosovo, and he replied what he replied and then General Ojdanic asked him if he could look at the map to see what this was about. He gave him the map and left. And the Chief of the Supreme Command staff studied the map and immediately called me. That is a part of the story from that testimony. If you would like me to go into more detail and to continue I can immediately answer or perhaps you can put a question, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So General Ojdanic got this map from General Pavkovic who had -- from Pavkovic who had just come from meeting Milosevic with the map?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he got the map from General Pavkovic directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, you testified in Milutinovic that the map had some writing on the top of it. And just to be clear on that, if we look at in the transcript, it's transcript page number 16977. And in the exhibit it is page 50, I believe, and you can just read it. You stated: "I cannot recall exactly the word order, but it was 'decision for operation.' And below that: 'Order of the Joint Command.' And as it says here: 'Strictly confidential,' number such-and-such." Do you recall that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know this strictly confidential number part. Yes, I do remember -- well, when I looked at the map as a professional, I could see that it was not the whole map, that it was an excerpt. Secondly, that in the left upper -- upper left-hand corner there was no name of the person who approved it. There was no name, rank, signature, or stamp, and in the lower right-hand corner there was no information about who drafted the map. There was no signature, no stamp, or anything like that. Then I paid attention to what was represented on the topographical map by the usual tactical markings and then I looked at the top exactly what that was, and that's where I read that this was a decision on action in the sector of Rogovo pursuant to a command by the commander, or rather the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, and there was some number, I think 148/ some other number, and that's what that -- and that's more or less what you are saying now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And referring back to P1236, are these suggestions that General Ojdanic came up with after reviewing this map with you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these suggestions were made after that short meeting in the corridor at the Supreme Command between the Chief of the General Staff and the 3rd Army commander. So that is an analysis of the situation on the map and what was stated on the map. I remember very well that there was no order. I state that the Chief of the Supreme Command staff did not have an order there that would be mentioned. When he wrote these suggestions, he had to refer back to some document that he had looked at in order to more easily direct the 3rd Army command as to what he was thinking when he was writing this, that's why.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So when you say there was no order, you mean the map did not have a corresponding order attached to it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, all I want to say is that us, we in the staff, the Supreme Command staff chief did not have that order. That is why he wrote these suggestions purely on the basis of the situation on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. But at the top of the map it did say, Order of the Joint Command, even though no other order, no typed up order was attached; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, if we look on this exhibit at P1236 where it says, "Link: Kosovo and Metohija Joint [Realtime translation read in error "Supreme"] Command Order, Strictly Confidential Number 455-148 of 15 April 1999," does this mean that these suggestions are referring to that order?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned the Supreme Command and some others, I don't know that, but I would like to look at the first page at least of this order in my language.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I think this is the first page. I'm just referring to the part that said "link."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, I have a technical intervention. When I read the text in Serbian, and when I look at the translation that is in English, I don't know whether it's a translation problem, but it doesn't state anywhere "super command" as it is in the transcript and I think the colleague is reading the English text, and I think the witness also pointed that out.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Actually, you are correct, the transcript is wrong. What the order says, what the exhibit says is link: Kosovo and Metohija Joint Command order. Not supreme command. Joint Command order, Strictly Confidential Number 455-148 of 15 April 1999."

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: General, does this mean that these suggestions are referring back to that Joint Command order with that strictly confidential number?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, once again absolutely not. I tried to explain that last time when I testified but evidently that was not a properly entered into the transcript, if this is what is happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Let me see if I can just clarify. I'm not asking you right now if General Ojdanic reviewed that other order. I'm just asking if this link means that this is making suggestions to this other order that it's referring to? Whether he looked at it or not, I'm not asking that question at this time. Does this mean link, this is related to that order, that other order?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, no. Why? He is writing his suggestions only on the basis of what he saw on the map and this title on the map, so he cannot write on the basis of some command without having seen it at all, and it cannot be understood in that way. We know what a command or an order looks like, and it would be even better if we could see this order somewhere and comment on it. So only on the basis of the situation on the map because I remember that Judge Bonomy had asked me whether I would be able to make suggestions like this or some other document only on the basis of the situation that you could see on the map. And I answered convincingly that I would, that I'm a trained officer with completed military education and that I'm capable only on the basis of what is entered on to the map to write even more suggestions than are what written here. This is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay, General, so your testimony is these suggestions have nothing do with Kosovo and Metohija Joint Command Order Strictly Confidential Number 455-148 dated 15 April 1999; is that what you are saying, or ...

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, other than the title, they have nothing to do with each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
