utterances.text: If we could now look at Exhibit P1328.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And if we look at the top of this document, we see that it says "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, Strictly Confidential Number 455-148, 15 April 1999." Would you agree, sir, that that is the same title, strictly confidential number, and date that are referred to in the suggestions document P1236?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree, but I would only kindly ask to look at the complete order in hard copy in order to be able to look at it if I'm expected to give any more answers regarding this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I think it's sufficient. You are agreeing that it's the same number, date, and title, your testimony is you do not believe that General Ojdanic saw this or referred to this; do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's sufficient in order to note that it's the same number, but I would like for the purposes of my testimony, for the purposes of the truth, to look at the complete order including the last page because only then can I provide valid testimony about this. The fact that it has the same number as over there at this point in time means nothing to me. I am convinced that it has nothing to do with others because here, for example, here underneath the title it says "map ratio 1:50.000, page 1, 2, 3, 4, that is an integral part of the order, and I would provide much better comments if I could look at the complete order if I'm to provide authentic testimony. And finally, I assert that this document was not in the General Staff at that time and was not provided to the Chief of the Supreme Command staff or to me. I have managed to look. I recall perhaps seeing it before two and a half years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And finally if we could just look quickly at Defence 65 ter 46 and those doc ID numbers are D006-0499.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that we are not going to look at this document anymore?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I think we understand your testimony. Your testimony is General Ojdanic did not look at the order, he only looked at the map that he had received from Pavkovic; is that a correct statement of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but I would like to add one more sentence and that is just like earlier when we were looking at some documents without a stamp or signature, as far as I'm concerned, this is not a valid document because it does not state who drafted it, who typed it, it does not contained the stamp or actually the name and the last name of the signature, so some elements are missing, and if I were the commander would receive such an order, I would simply put it aside and would not react. I would ask to receive a proper order from the person who was my superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: General, you would agree this is not a VJ document, it's a Joint Command document; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless, I would not agree with that because I can see here only military units that are listed. Thus, the assignment was issued to the 125th Motorised Brigade. That is a unit of the army. I don't see that some other unit was given an assignment because it does not state that here, so that no one can issue assignments to a military unit other than a military commander regardless of what is said at the beginning or in the body of the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: General, I believe if you look at point 2 in this order, it does say the Pristina Corps with the reinforced and armed non-Siptar population of KiM is to support MUP forces in breaking up and destroying the SDS in the zone of responsibility; does it not say that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the assignment received by the Pristina Corps from the 3rd Army and then it is talking about its assignment further on, so this is something else. The only task to the establishment units in article or paragraph 5.1 is given to the 125th Motorised Brigade for us professional soldiers. This indicates without any doubt that is an assignment issued to a military unit to keep MUP units in the implementation of an assignment. There are -- or to support military units in the implementation of an assignment. There are no other assignments. And I believe that this is a classic document of the Pristina Corps entered in the log-book of the Pristina Corps which does have the markings of the Joint Command but does not contain the signature or stamp of any command, neither the Joint Command nor the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right, sir. If it we look quickly at 65 ter 46.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could have that up on the screen, D006-0499. And if we could just go in the English to page 4, paragraph 6 and in the B/C/S to page 3, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I apologise, I don't see much, and I insist on a hard copy because I'm really unable to read here what you would like me to read. I don't see the date, I don't see what this is about. All I see is just blurry text.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I just need you to look at paragraph 6 if we could.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very gladly, but you need to tell me what this document is, what is the date, and everything else for me to be able to say something.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Could we look at the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please zoom in at the top of the page so that I could see what the date is. Yes, I see now what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Can I please see it in English also.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So, sir, I just want to confirm with you at paragraph 6 that this is just seeking confirmation that that telegram with the suggestions was sent. Is that what that is?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I know that it wasn't, but still, I would like to look at this text and have it in front of me. Every evening -- just the last point that you are referring to. I don't need to have a hard copy, just if you can zoom in the relevant part on the screen for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir. So we can see that this is a briefing of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command on April 18th, 1999, and in paragraph 6 of it, if we could go back to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Page 4, paragraph 6 in English; page 3, paragraph 6 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: It says: "Lieutenant-General Curcin find out when the telegram was sent to the 3rd Army command and when the telegram was delivered." I'm not asking if it was delivered, I'm just asking if these minutes reflect that you were asked to find out that information?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, this is the evening briefing at the command about the situation at the front, primarily in the Pristina Corps area, and we can see that they are discussing all the members are, and at the end it says closing address by the Chief of the Supreme Command. So he is precisely issuing instructions to everybody and he is issuing this assignment to me that you have just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. And he is referring back to that telegram that we looked at, Exhibit 1236, correct, his suggestions dated April 17th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because there was a problem about delivery, non-delivery, what he wrote was not respected, and he asked that it be exactly established when it was sent, when it was received, when it was delivered and a few days later we do have a report from the 3rd Army commander about this. And I also reported once I had established what had happened here to the Supreme Command staff chief about all of that because the problem is broader here than what is said in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. And we don't need to get into that today.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could just tender 65 ter 46, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be received as Exhibit P01523. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, General, when you were looking at this map with General Ojdanic and at the top of it that said Joint Command order, did he say at any point, who is this Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask about it nor was there any mention of it at the previous meeting. We were interested in the tactical situations, the indications we had, and the assignments of the forces represented on the map, and since it was not map, there was no approved at the top, nor indication who produced it at the bottom, I had in reason to ask about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you if you asked about, I'm asking if during the time you were looking at this map with General Ojdanic if he said, Who is this Joint Command at the top of this map?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've already said in my previous answer that it was not mentioned once in that evening discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. Yesterday you were asked questions about the resubordination of the MUP to the VJ. Do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the topic and most of the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: General, the resubordination order from President Milosevic - D203, I believe - General Ojdanic never sent this to the Ministry of the Interior; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know the numbers by heart. You mean the order of President Milosevic or his order?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: The order of President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now. General Ojdanic did not have the authority to send a telegram like this on behalf of President Milosevic and his military office, that's why there was the military office headed by Colonel Susic. This telegram under the name of the president could not be sent by General Ojdanic to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So just to be clear, he did not -- he did not forward this to the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I insist on the expression I used. He did not have -- he was not in charge of sending, forwarding such things. He did not have the authority. Somebody else from the office of the president had that authority. So the answer is no, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And your testimony in Milutinovic was that the MUP was never actually resubordinated to the VJ in the end, correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that from that previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd like to talk to you a little bit now about the incident at Racak. I don't know if we need to call these exhibits up, we'll see how it goes. But yesterday there was reference to two exhibits. There was one, which I believe is D556, which was a request for a report on where the -- on whether the Pristina Corps had been involved in the Racak incident. Do you recall discussing that, General?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And there is D557, which was a report back up saying that no, that the VJ had not been involved; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This telegram was one I drafted on the orders of the Chief of the General Staff and the reply came that same night from the 3rd Army which had received its answer from the Pristina Corps saying that the army was not involved in that incident, as you call it, in Racak.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, General, you yourself were not on the ground in Racak; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. So what you know about it, you know from this report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We trusted our commanders as they trusted us, and when they are explicitly ordered to provide a reply bearing full criminal, moral, and other liability, putting their signatures on it, then they reply. This was not broadcast because of possible media manipulations and because of claims by certain verifiers that 40 artillery shells had been fired at Racak and to deny it had to be written like --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I need to stop you there because my question for you was simply this is the extent of your knowledge about Racak, correct, this report is the basis of your knowledge; correct? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, were you aware that international observers monitored the incident at Racak on 15th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it from the media. I also heard about it at the Milutinovic et al. trial, but I also know that it was a tangentious report that was not truthful. I mean, their claims were not truthful. And plus, I'm wondering why Racak is not in this indictment, in the indictment against Milutinovic and others, if it's accurate. President Milosevic proved that it was a staged incident --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there, and I'll be asking you the questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could just look at P1250.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, looking just below the date, this report was -- oh, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first, this is from a website we don't know when it was created and when it was updated. Second, their translation is not correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Djurdjic, you have to wait, the questions will be put and answered, and then if you have a comment, you can make it. You remember this is the concern that I've expressed several times when you are suggesting possible answers before the witness has an opportunity to deal with the matter. We will hear you later. At the moment now, the witness should carry on answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: General, if you look at this report, it's from the -- it's an update from the Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission, and it states just starting right after the date: "US KDOM observed the FRY police/military attack on the Racak-Petrovo-Malopoljce area throughout the day on January 15th. VJ armoured units and mortars fired into the villages, with at least three tank rounds visibly hitting civilian houses. Fires started by the shelling burned in the villages for several hours after the attack." Sir, were you aware that international observers saw VJ armoured units and mortars fire into the village of Racak?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand any of this because I don't have a translation. All of this is in English. On the left side and on the right side as well. Second, I understand your question. KDOM was a separate American mission that was never subordinated to the OSCE Mission. It acted independently. I know that much. Second, I knew mainly from the media that they claimed what we see here, but reading carefully the reply of the 3rd Army, it says that one tank platoon, that means three tanks, had been in the area, they had been carrying out certain activities, and they were attacked. Fire ensued from the surrounding hills and elevations. They stopped, organised themselves for defence, and fired a number of projectiles. The exact number is in the report of the 3rd Army, broken down by calibres. They assert they had not targeted Racak village but instead opened fire at the forces which from two elevations were firing at them in self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I don't believe that report says that the fire was coming from inside the village of Racak, does it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military unit couldn't have known that for sure because they were not around Racak or in Racak. They were fired at from the surrounding hills, not from Racak village. So they returned enemy fire outside Racak village. If you are kind enough, you will read during the break the report of the 3rd Army in detail and you will see that the report says something different. So nobody can accuse the army of firing upon Racak village.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, in the KDOM update, the observers state that they witnessed firsthand at least three tank rounds visibly hit civilian homes in Racak. Now, assuming that these troops were fired upon from the hills, is it an appropriate response to shoot tank rounds into the village of Racak?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that these three shells were fired at Racak village? I never said that. And I maintain and the 3rd Army commander maintains that artillery and tanks never fired at Racak village. If you understand me correctly, then that answers your question. Plus I don't see that this is a very fresh date. What January is it? 15, 16, no, it's 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: You are correct, sir, it's an update with dates of multiple things included. But, sir, my question to you was not whether you had stated that tanks fired into Racak. I'm putting to you that this KDOM update states: "VJ armoured units and mortars fired into the villages with at least three tank rounds visibly hitting civilian houses." My question to you is, if these -- if this unit was fired upon from the hills, is it an appropriate response to fire with tanks into a village hitting civilian homes, towards civilian homes?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say once again there was no fire opened at Racak. Did I understand you correctly as saying that these shells seen by KDOM were fired at Racak? I have to understand that first in order to be able to reply. I did not understand from what is written here that they were claiming that. They did hear, maybe they even saw shells, but not a single shell fell on Racak village. Another thing, not here, not anywhere do we see a definition of proportionate response, but if somebody is firing at the army from nearby elevations, are these soldiers supposed to fan out and go chasing their attackers through the woods? This is how it happened that they responded to fire and the moment that they fired back, the fire from the elevation stopped as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, is it proper to respond to small arms fire with tank fire?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If necessary, but I maintain that there was not just infantry fire. In the report of the 3rd Army command, they say exactly which weapons had been used to fire at them. It was not just infantry weapons, as you say.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And, sir, just one more question on this. Your assertion that no shells fell on Racak, again that's not based on your own observation, that's solely based on this report; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the report of the 3rd Army, and I believe the commander of the 3rd Army and the Chief of Staff that they provided a perfectly honest answer. That would not have dared to play with the truth because the international public was already outraged and there were quarrels with Mr. Walker. The Chief of the General Staff wanted the truth, whatever it was. On the 21st of January, at the meeting, you can see that, and at later meetings as well. It was not in our interest to lie.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, it certainly wasn't in the interest of the VJ to be seen as being involved in the Racak incident, was it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If it had been necessary, maybe we would have gotten involved, but then the reports would have reflected that and would have specified how the army was involved, but I maintain once again, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a new area to go into, so if it's probably a good time to take the break right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Let me first ask Mr. Djurdjic, is there a matter he now wishes to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the course of this trial, I've learned some things and I never make objections during a cross-examination by the other party except procedural. But we would have wasted a lot less time with this document if we had received it in good time. The Prosecution sent us this document three minutes before 8.00 p.m., and the search engine of Mr. Stamp was repaired a few days ago. These documents should really not be used in this way and notified belatedly when the Defence had no longer any time to prepare. I believe we should be given documents to be used in cross-examination 24 hours earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As you are aware, Mr. Djurdjic, that is the order and the procedure to be followed. And if there is a variation from that, leave needs to be sought, as you yourself sought on a number of occasions. Anything by way of observation, Ms. Petersen?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First, this is a document that is in evidence, and it's been in evidence for quite a while, so the document itself is not new. I'm not sure of the exact date, but I believe it was in August of this year that the document was tendered. So this is not a new document. And also, we have -- maybe we should improve our practices but both the Defence and the Prosecution have been somewhat flexible with each other if a document that one of us wants to use the Defence have availed themselves of this with their direct examination, and yes, I did make a decision to use this document yesterday and noticed it as soon as I made that decision, although our notice was sent within the 24-hour period. This was something that was later added, but both sides have been flexible with each other in doing this. If the Defence no longer wants to have that practice we can have a discussion, but we have been flexible with one another in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's no reason for any further particular comment from the Chamber in respect of this exhibit. The point raised is simply that there was not notice that an exhibit would be used in cross-examination. As both parties are aware of documents that are exhibited, that is not a serious breach of courtesy. If Mr. Djurdjic is in some difficulty in respect of re-examination about the document, he can raise that specifically with us, and we'll consider it. We will now have the second break and resume at 3 minutes past 1.00. [The witness stands down]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to move to a new topic now. Yesterday you were asked about training that you received in international humanitarian law. Do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And you went to a training at Topcider Barracks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean that last one round in September 1998 or December 1998, yes, but we had many training courses before. When we had the first workshop based on the agreement between the minister of defence and his counter-parts at the ICRC we organised these workshops, and I had occasion to organise the first such workshop in the 1st Army. We all received certificates of instructors, and all these instructors had the obligation at corps level and at the brigade level to conduct similar workshops and all the officers down to brigade level had the obligation to go through such a course and become instructors. And on the 25th of November 1998 was the last workshop attending by representatives of the ICRC who came to greet us and to work with us for three days. I can tell you more about it if you were interested.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: When was the first training, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the first one -- the first workshop was in 1996 at the command of the 1st Army, and then across other strategic groups, training was held on orders of the Chief of the General Staff. And each of these workshops was attended by appropriate representatives of the ICRC including the head of mission in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: When you say "ICRC" you are referring to the Red Cross; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's the acronym.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you take this training seriously?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I personally took it very seriously and participated and made every effort to learn as much as possible and to teach my subordinates, and I received great praise from the representatives of the International Red Cross, and I have to say that all our offices from all levels took this training very seriously, the training in international humanitarian law and devoted great attention to implementation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And do you think forces, both police or military, if people in the police or military violate international humanitarian law or commit a war crime, do you think they should be punished?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that everywhere in the world, including in our country, anyone who violates international humanitarian law should be punished, be it a serviceman or a civilian or a member of the Ministry of the Interior. But that should apply everywhere in the world, that is my deep conviction.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Do you know Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And how long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to give me a moment to remember because I didn't know I would be faced with questions like this. I know him from the time when we served at the command staff academy and then went to our units. It could have been in the 1970s. And in the same brigade we served in Macedonia in the 3rd Army as battalion commanders. And later on we were friends and our families were friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: General, are you aware that Mladic has been indicted by this Tribunal for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it, and I know, if I can believe the media, and Mr. Harmon made a point of making me aware of it. He is the prosecuting attorney I met in Belgrade once and again in end March last year when I testified before this court. I haven't seen the indictment though and I don't know any details.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, are you aware that the charges in the indictment against Mladic include that he slaughtered over 7.000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to hear and read about it in electronic and printed media over the past years.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, based on your training in international humanitarian law, you would agree that that charge -- not asking you your belief about whether it's true or not, but you believe that that charge alleges a violation of the rules that you learned about in your training, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And, sir, are you aware that there is an international arrest warrant for Mladic and that there has been for quite sometime?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, conditionally speaking, I could say yes, although I haven't seen the indictment, and the media have reported all sorts of things, and there was a time when it was the talk of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you familiar with two Yugoslav Army facilities called Rajac and Stragari?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know these two military installations, Stragari and Rajac.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And these are both VJ facilities; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received interpretation that seems to refer to some sort of buildings, I need clarification because at Rajac there's only a hotel open to the public, and free weekend cottages. The other one is more built up but again there are no major buildings. Not in the sense that we use the word building, edifice.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Are these facilities of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in the army, they belonged to the VJ, but they served as special purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, at Rajac, not just a soldier would be allowed to stay there, correct, you'd have to be an officer if you wanted to say at Rajac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. It's a hotel open to the public, there is a price list in the Official Gazette listing tariffs for overnight stay, lunches, dinners, full board, et cetera. Anyone can book, not only military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: But it was owned by the VJ, correct, sir? It's a VJ facility?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just like some spas across Serbia such as Vrnjacka Banja and other places across Yugoslavia, and on the coast we used to have resorts and hotels on the seashore, on mountains. Those were recreation and rest facilities for military personnel and for civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, did you visit with Mladic at both of these facilities beginning in 1997?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall, but there is a statement I've given to the OTP and my testimony, you probably know that, and if you jog my memory, I'll confirm or deny. We did meet a couple of times in public places, at these facilities, but I can also tell you we went once one night to the football match between Yugoslavia and Croatia, and we watched it together at the stadium of the Red Star Football Team in Belgrade. I don't know if I was asked about that last time, but if I wasn't, I'm volunteering the information now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter 06031. This is the testimony of this witness in the Perisic trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And if we turn to page 18 of the exhibit, sir, on page 18 you were asked: "General Curcin, did you see General Mladic at the Rajac facility?" "Yes," you answered. Question: "When did you see General Mladic at the facility?" Answer: "In early July of 1997." And then on line 7 you said you couldn't remember exactly but you were sure you saw him at least once -- approximately one month later. Does that refresh your memory about the number of times you saw him at Rajac?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there's nothing contentious there, as far as I am concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And on page 26 of this transcript you visited him again at Rajac much later. Does that refresh your memory that you visited him again at the Rajac facility?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I know that I did visit him, but I don't know when, what month, what year. I know that we did see each other at least one more time at Rajac, and I know probably what your next question will be and that is at one occasion when we were there General Perisic simply also dropped by. If that is your following question, he just stopped by in his private capacity just like myself, and we briefly met there. This is also in the transcript although I didn't have the opportunity to look at the transcript either in Serbian or in preparation for my testimony today, but I do remember, and I'm sure you will help me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, actually my next question for you is still about the Rajac facility. One of your tasks around the time that Mladic stayed there was to make it more liveable there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. This is a very clumsily put by the director of the training centre Corporal 1st Class Gujn [phoen], and it seemed to him that the assistance became more intensive after or when I visited Rajac on one occasion. I'm going to explain. The army command had decided to rent out that facility so investments had to be made, civilian sheets and blankets had to be procured, at least one woman had to be hired for housekeeping. We needed to buy washing machine and dishwasher and also some equipment for cutting the grass because the facility was a little bit neglected. All of this began a little bit earlier because this was discussed at the collegium of the 1st Army command under whose jurisdiction this facility was, and that really has nothing do with Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you if on page 13 of the transcript we are looking at, did you not say when referring to your task with regard to Rajac: "What I meant was the internal division between me and the logistics assistant who it was to be between the two of us who would take care of facilities to make them liveable for the people who go to rest there." So did you not have a role in making the Rajac facility liveable for the people went to rest there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that is what I said, but that is not what I meant. What I meant was that it was necessary for the two of us in some way to divide our duties, and I'm going to tell you why now. I'm not going to ask for a closed session because the facility was --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I just want to know if you performed that task or not, if you played any role in that task?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot answer you in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: You will not tell us if you played that role or not?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do -- well, I don't have the right not -- well, I don't have the right to not reply because I was create problems for me, for my family, bring shame upon myself or criminal prosecution, but since I see that you are very persistent, I'm going to tell you that this began much earlier. We received the assignments much earlier from the 1st Army command to renovate these facilities because this was the place where our commands went in case of an alarm, some sort of alert or emergency or danger of war. In such a situation we would directly go to these facilities, the logistics of the 1st Army went to Stragari, and the command went to Rajac. Since I was in charge of that operation section, then I took it upon myself to bring it up to such state that you could immediately go and use those facilities and not for somebody to come from the outside or for a foreign country or something to be able to rest there. So this is actually a much broader explanation than I think the one that you requested of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And after your renovation Mladic stayed there; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assure you that the renovation began much before that and that the renovation was carried out according to the funds we had at our disposal. I don't know when he went there and how long he stayed. Others went there too, and I also spent at least seven days each year there, of course, and I paid for it, and I'm still keeping all the bills or invoices that I paid for each of my stays there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: General, did you continue seeing Mladic up until 2002?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did see each other a few times up until January -- early January 2002, and from that time on we definitely never met one another again. I testified about that in detail and it is in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. So during this time that you would see Mladic, from 1997 to 2002, at that time were you aware that there was an indictment from this Tribunal and a warrant for his arrest for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear somewhat later about that from the media, as well as the reward that was published for anyone who would assist in his capture.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And, sir, did you not tell others at the Rajac facility that they were not to tell anyone else about Mladic's visits to the facility?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That is what it says in the transcripts from my previous testimony in March last year.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And, General, this was to assist Mladic in evading arrest on the charges of this Tribunal, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I'm concerned. Simply there was the danger that choppers or helicopters from Bosnia or in some other way NATO that had its forces there could suddenly come, violate our air-space, and capture and hand over General Mladic. Secondly, there were some renegade groups in our country, members of some other forces there, who could also do something like that. We did have a case of one of our citizens being kidnapped somewhere on a mountain and then he was transported across the river Drina and handed over, so the idea was, and I talked about that, was to prevent any harm from happening to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I believe your testimony was just that the reason you told people not to say where Mladic was is that there was a danger that choppers or helicopters from Bosnia or in some other way NATO that had its forces there could suddenly come, violate our air-space and capture and hand over General Mladic, meaning arrest and hand over General Mladic to the custody of this Tribunal to face the charges against him; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you could understand it that way too. I'm not denying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, after the Law on Co-Operation with the Tribunal was passed in 2002, since that time and at that time you did not inform anyone of any of the information you have about the whereabouts of General Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, namely the last time I saw him was sometime between the 7th and the 14th of January 2002. Already I was retired by that time. The law was passed in April. After this date when the law went into effect, I did not see or hear or communicate with General Mladic again. So I couldn't really then report having any kind of contact with him either.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: But in 2002, you didn't turn over to authorities any information that you had up until that time about places he went or where he might be?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the Perisic case, if we could turn to page 83, line 16. Judge David asked you: "You said also that you had not received orders to inform the presence of General Mladic in your statement today. Had you received orders to do so, to reveal his presence, would you have done so because of your friendship and relations to the general?" And your answer was: "I do not know who would issue such an order, but I would never reveal my information about this, not on any cost." General, as you sit here today, that's still true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what somebody would perhaps like to say in answer to this question. I'm a serious man, a general, and I gave my solemn statement at the beginning of the testimony. Perhaps it would be fit for me to say at this moment that I would very gladly report him and seriously very sincerely, I did think a lot from last March until now what would happen were I to know, and I must say in response to your quite definite question that I am today also saying that I would not report, hand over, or extradite General Mladic were I to know where he was at any price. So since this is a hypothetical question, my answer is also a hypothetical one.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And your answer is no, correct, you would not? You would not turn him over?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you were asked questions about the combat reports yesterday. Do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honours, I would like to tender the transcript from the Perisic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Just those pages, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, it would really be up to the Court. I'm not sure if you would prefer to have the context of the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't want to receive the whole of the transcript of the Perisic trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Those pages are fine then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, oh, yes, just this testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's received as Exhibit Number P01524. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I am not mistaken, these are just answers to specific questions. This is not my entire testimony. These are questions taken out of context of the entire testimony, but I don't have a problem to have this admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I'd like to talk to you about the combat reports that you spoke about yesterday. Looking at your statement, your witness statement, which I believe is D553.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could look at paragraph 9. And if we could just go to paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right, sir, in paragraph 9 you discuss that you have studied all of these combat reports. I assume these are the ones that are now in evidence in this case; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't managed to read paragraph 9, so if you can just kindly zoom in on that paragraph, if that's all you are interested in this report, because I would just like to remind myself a little bit. I don't need to read everything in detail. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Yes, and it is your statement in this document that in these reports there are no reports of any VJ officer taking away identity documents; is that correct? I'm sorry, I should be more precise, any members of the Pristina Corps taking away any identity documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And there are no reports of attacks on the civilian population; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: No reports on mass killings?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. There were no reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: No reports on the deportation of the Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as a topic and not deportation. First of all, let's see if we are thinking of the same thing. Deportation is one thing, internal refugees are something else, and the population leaving on its own is something else. If I remember well, nowhere was any kind of deportation of civilians organised from Kosovo. This was not in any report either.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. And there is no report of deliberate destruction of religious buildings, is that also what you are telling us in paragraph 9?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were no reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And if we look at paragraph 22, you speak again about this, here you say that there are no reports of ethnic cleansing, correct, in these reports, in these combat reports?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. No reports of looting or torching and destroying property also?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says mass looting, nothing about mass or large-scale looting, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. Now, so if we were to go through all of these combat reports that are in evidence now, we wouldn't find any reports of any of those things; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I state. That is how it is. Individual cases, individual killings in some place two or three, for example in Kosovo Polje were mentioned, but all of these things were processed. What was under the jurisdiction of the corps command and the army command, that was discovered and reported was also something that was dealt with, processed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, just to clarify, do these reports contain reporting about MUP activities?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which reports you mean. The Supreme Command staff ones or the ones by the 3rd Army command?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I mean the combat reports that came into evidence that you were shown yesterday and you spoke of, those combat reports that went up to the Supreme Command, were those reporting --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Supreme Command staff?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: The ones that went to the Supreme Command staff, I believe.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, these are distinctions but very important ones. There are two reports, reports that reached the Supreme Command staff, and an integral combat report which the Supreme Command staff submitted to the supreme commander each morning. I don't know which ones you mean. According to the list that was discussed this morning, I assume that you mean the combat reports of the Supreme Command staff, so please, could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm referring to what you're referring to in your statement. You said you reviewed combat reports and they don't contain reports of any of these things in them. I'm asking you if those reports you're referred to, if they report on the MUP or just the VJ?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they could not contain detailed information about the MUP because this is a different structure, it had a different chain of command. The reports referred to events in their own ranks and maybe sometimes incidentally there would be a sentence about some unit of the 3rd Army of the Pristina Corps supported MUP units in the implementation of some assignment, that could have been in the reports, yes. Otherwise, there were no detailed reports about what the MUP did. It was not part of their duty to have to do that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Sir, now I'd like to speak to you about the plans and orders that came down from the General Staff or the Supreme Command staff. I want to make sure I have your testimony clear. Your testimony is that you were in the unit in charge of drafting all of these orders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes, I was at the head of the administration, that mainly was entrusted in peacetime and war time with writing commands, orders, reports and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And your testimony is knowing of all the plans that were drafted, there was no plan to expel the civilian population; is that correct? And I'm also referring here to your statement at paragraph 20, that there has never been a plan to expel -- to assist or support terror and violence against the Albanian civilian population; is that correct? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, all these things that we just discussed, mass killings, deportation, destroying religious sites, based on your training in international humanitarian law, you understand that those would be war crimes; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I don't understand the question, I didn't speak about that, I didn't say that that there were any deportations, mass killings, crimes and so on and so forth. This is what I think you mentioned and asked for my view, but I claim that this was not contained in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I understand it's your testimony that it's not in the reports. Those activities would be considered a war crime if they took place; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a hypothetical question, and I'm going to give a hypothetical answer, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you based on all of the training that you received in international humanitarian law, your opinion about whether these would constitute war crimes, your understanding about whether these are war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like the statements to be presented correctly, especially if they are being read out, and I think a document is being read out. My learned friend said just now that religious facilities and other things, other crimes, were not referred to in the reports. It says in the statement: "I state with full responsibility that in the Army of Yugoslavia or the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia there was never any kind of plan, order, or anything which in any way supported or instigated any type of crimes against the Albanian population." I don't want to read the entire thing. All I wanted to say is that what is being presented by the Prosecutor at this case is incorrect, and if it is being presented, I would then kindly ask that it be done correctly because what is stated in paragraph 20 has nothing to do with the combat reports that were the topic of questions a little bit before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I believe we've moved on from combat reports, Mr. Djurdjic. Carry on, please, Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I do note the time. I'm on my last topic, I would guess depending on the speed here it could be done in the next 10 or 15 minutes if we want to push through so the witness can leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm afraid we must adjourn now. There is another trial sitting in the courtroom at 2:15. So we must give them half an hour to change over. That means we must now adjourn to resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 5th day of February, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.
